name: The Halo Effect
statement: One good impression bleeds into judgements of unrelated traits.
statementAccent: bleeds into judgements of unrelated traits
meaning: An overall impression of a person — that they are attractive, likeable, or generally good — biases judgements of their specific, logically unrelated qualities such as intelligence, competence, or honesty. A single favourable characteristic, or a diffuse positive feeling, colours ratings of attributes that have nothing to do with it.
mechanism: A global affective impression of the target is formed first, or alongside, and that general good-or-bad feeling then suffuses ratings of specific qualities. Raters fail to evaluate each trait independently; the overall impression constrains the specific judgements, producing artificially high correlations between logically distinct traits. The rater experiences the judgements as separate and objective, but they are driven by one underlying gut feeling — often without awareness.

examples.text: Thorndike found commanding officers rating soldiers gave implausibly correlated scores across unrelated traits like physique, intelligence, and leadership, as if one general sense of merit coloured every specific rating.

In a classic study, more physically attractive people were assumed to have more desirable personalities and better life prospects — the attractiveness halo extending to traits it cannot logically imply.

Students shown the same instructor portrayed as warm rated his appearance, mannerisms, and accent as appealing, while those told he was cold found the very same features irritating — and were unaware the overall impression drove their ratings.

variants.name: The horn effect
variants.text: The negative counterpart, in which one unfavourable impression drags down ratings of unrelated traits — also called the reverse halo, devil, or pitchfork effect.

variants.name: The brand halo
variants.text: The marketing extension in which a favourable impression of one product or attribute lifts perception of a whole brand — or a single flaw sours judgement of everything else.

whyItMatters: It is a foundational bias in social perception, distorting hiring, appraisals, teaching evaluations, jury judgements, and consumer choices wherever an overall impression contaminates specific assessments. It shows how poorly people separate distinct qualities, and why structured, criterion-by-criterion evaluation is needed to counter it.

working.text: when evaluating someone, assess each quality on its own evidence rather than letting a general impression carry over.
be alert that charm or good looks may be inflating your judgement of unrelated competence or character.
since the bias operates unawares, do not trust your sense that your judgements were independent — build in structure instead.

limits: The effect is robust and widely replicated, but it is fundamentally a bias in ratings, not a claim that the traits really covary — the inflated correlations are the artefact. People are typically unaware of the halo's influence, so self-report cannot detect or correct it, and forewarning does not reliably remove it. Effect sizes and moderators vary with culture, context, and domain: the direction is general, but which specific traits get attributed from a positive impression differs across settings.
misreadings: It does not mean attractive or likeable people really are more competent — it means observers wrongly infer that they are. And it is not something people can simply introspect their way out of; the influence operates below awareness, and being warned about it is not enough.
origin: Named and first empirically demonstrated by Edward Thorndike in 'A Constant Error in Psychological Ratings,' Journal of Applied Psychology 4(1):25-29 (1920), from officers rating soldiers.

sources.text: Halo effect, Wikipedia. — the impression-suffusing statement, Thorndike's 1920 study, the beauty and warm-lecturer examples, and the horn effect.
